Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Advanced Network Troubleshooting
Advanced Network Troubleshooting
A practical, layered workflow for diagnosing connectivity, name resolution, routing, firewall, and socket-level problems.
In this lesson

You will follow a step-by-step diagnostic flow using ip, ping, dig, ip r, traceroute, ss and firewall-cmd, then see how to automate those checks with Ansible.

Why it matters

Network problems often surface as application failures. A structured approach reduces mean time to repair and prevents risky ad-hoc changes that can cause outages.

Explore Key Topics
Interface & Connectivity
Use ip a and ping to confirm interfaces and basic reachability; bring links up when necessary.
DNS & Routing
dig, nslookup and ip r/traceroute help separate name problems from path or gateway issues.
Firewall & Sockets
firewall-cmd and ss show whether ports are allowed and services are listening.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
16:9 HD Classroom
Troubleshooting Flow
Interface → Connectivity → DNS → Routing → Firewall → Sockets
Automate with Ansible
Capture the same checks as playbooks to run across many hosts.
Safe Testing
Try firewall changes temporarily before making them permanent and reload when ready.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Learning Objectives
01 • Interfaces
Use ip a to list addresses and ip link set interface up to bring a link online. This is the first step whenever a host is unreachable.
02 • Routing
Read ip r for the kernel routing table and use traceroute to locate where path breaks occur between local and remote hosts.
03 • Sockets (ss)
Run ss -tunap to confirm listening sockets, associated processes, and unexpected socket states that can explain failed connections.

Write playbooks to gather network facts, run dig, verify ports, and list firewalld rules so diagnostics are consistent across your fleet.

screens.title: Start with interfaces and addresses
screens.narratorSegment: A basic but crucial diagnostic step is to confirm the local interface state and assigned IP addresses. The command ip a lists each interface, its operational state and configured addresses. Look for the keywords UP or DOWN and for the presence of an expected IPv4 or IPv6 address. If the interface is down you can bring it online with ip link set up. This fixes many simple problems caused by administrative shutdowns, cable issues that have been corrected, or virtual interfaces that were not brought up after a reboot. A common misconception is to assume an interface is up because the service is running; interfaces and services are separate layers. Another frequent oversight is relying on NetworkManager UI without checking the kernel view; ip a shows the kernel's truth. Example: if a web server has no IP address on eth0, adding the address or bringing eth0 up restores reachability and lets you move to the next diagnostic step. After confirming the interface and address, always re-run a connectivity test such as ping to a known good IP. Key takeaway: interface state is the simplest and fastest elimination check before investigating name resolution or routing.

keyIdea.title: Interface first

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Start with interfaces and addresses
Definition
ip a / ip link
Use these commands to see the kernel view of interfaces, their state, and assigned addresses. The kernel's view determines actual connectivity.
$ ip a
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP> mtu 65536 qdisc noqueue state UNKNOWN
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST> mtu 1500 qdisc fq_codel state DOWN
    link/ether 52:54:00:12:34:56
If eth0 is DOWN, bring it up:
$ ip link set eth0 up
$ ip a
Supporting points
  • ip a shows the kernel's configured addresses and operational states.
  • ip link set can change the link state immediately, but persistent config may need nmcli or network scripts.
  • Always re-test connectivity after changing interface state.
Concrete example
A server with eth0 DOWN after maintenance is fixed by bringing the link up and confirming the expected IPv4 address, restoring service reachability.
Key Takeaway

Interface state is the fastest elimination step. If the interface is down or missing an IP, higher-layer diagnostics are misleading.

screens.title: Connectivity: ping and interpreting results
screens.narratorSegment: Ping is a basic but powerful tool to check reachability. Use ping to test an IP address first; if that succeeds but pinging a hostname fails, the issue is name resolution. This simple contrast often points directly at DNS. When ping to an IP works, you know the physical path is available and the default gateway and routing likely allow packets out. If ping to an IP fails, investigate the interface, the gateway, and traceroute to find where packets stop. A common misconception is to treat ping failures as proof that the remote host is down; intermediate firewalls or ICMP filtering can block ping while TCP services remain accessible. So, combine ping with a TCP test such as nc -zvw3 host port if ICMP is filtered. Example: you can ping 8.8.8.8 to verify external reachability; if that succeeds but ping example. com fails, use dig against a DNS server to further investigate. Always follow ping with auxiliary checks that test the specific service protocol when ICMP might be blocked. How will you decide whether to test ICMP, DNS, or TCP first in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Ping for triage
keyIdea.text: Ping an IP to confirm packet delivery, then test a hostname to check DNS; follow up with TCP checks when ICMP is filtered.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Connectivity: ping
Process
Ping IP → Ping hostname → TCP test
Start with an IP. If that works, the network path is healthy and name resolution is suspect. If the IP fails, trace the path with traceroute and check routing.
$ ping -c 4 8.8.8.8
$ ping -c 4 example.com
$ nc -zvw3 example.com 80  # TCP port check
Supporting points
  • Successful ping to an IP isolates DNS as the likely cause of a hostname failure.
  • ICMP may be filtered; follow up with TCP checks to verify service reachability.
  • Ping timing and loss percentages give clues about latency and packet loss during triage.
Concrete scenario
If web clients fail to load a site, ping the server IP. If that succeeds, run dig against your DNS server. If dig fails, update /etc/resolv.conf or flush local caches before changing firewall rules.
Key Takeaway

Use ping as a quick triage. Pair it with name and TCP checks to accurately isolate DNS, path, or service-level issues.

screens.title: DNS Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: DNS issues are a frequent source of application failures because services cannot reach hostnames even when IP connectivity exists. Start by inspecting /etc/resolv. conf to confirm which servers the host will query. If entries are missing or point to unreachable servers, update them or use a specific server for testing. Next, query DNS servers directly with dig or nslookup to verify what the server returns. For example, running dig against a known DNS server isolates whether resolution fails locally or at the server. If dig returns no answer, the DNS server may be misconfigured or unreachable. Local caching can also cause stale answers; use systemd-resolve --flush-caches to clear it when you suspect outdated records. A common misconception is to blame the application when hostnames fail; often the problem is a misconfigured resolver or an unreachable DNS server. Example: if clients cannot resolve api. example. com but resolver shows 127.0.0.53, test dig +short api. example. com @8.8.8.8 to confirm global resolution. Always pair DNS tests with connectivity checks so you know whether DNS or the network path is the root cause.

keyIdea.title: DNS triage
keyIdea.text: Verify resolv.conf, query specific DNS servers with dig or nslookup, and flush caches when results look stale.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › DNS Troubleshooting
Definition
DNS resolution diagnostics
Check resolv.conf for configured nameservers, query servers directly, and clear local caches when results disagree with expectation.
$ cat /etc/resolv.conf
$ dig +short api.example.com @8.8.8.8
$ nslookup api.example.com 8.8.8.8
$ systemd-resolve --flush-caches
Supporting points
  • /etc/resolv.conf controls the resolver the system will use unless a local resolver overrides it.
  • dig and nslookup let you test individual servers and see authoritative responses or failures.
  • Local caching can hide recent DNS changes; flushing resolves that mismatch during tests.
Concrete example
If an application reports name resolution failures but ping to the IP succeeds, run dig against a public resolver to check whether the hostname maps to an IP globally or if the problem is your local resolver chain.
Key Takeaway

DNS can look like a network outage. Test resolvers directly and flush caches to ensure results are current and accurate.

screens.title: Routing and traceroute
screens.narratorSegment: Routing determines where packets go once they leave your host. Use ip r to inspect the kernel routing table and verify the presence of a default route, typically shown as 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to a gateway. If external hosts are unreachable but local hosts are fine, a missing or incorrect default route is a likely cause. Traceroute helps you locate the hop where packets fail by showing each router along the path and the associated latency. It is particularly valuable for diagnosing problems outside your immediate network, such as an overloaded router or a blocked path. A common misconception is to assume symmetric routing; in reality, routing can differ in return path and an upstream filter may block traffic unevenly. Example: if ip r shows no default gateway, add a temporary route to test connectivity or use NetworkManager tools to persist the change. After identifying the failing hop with traceroute, coordinate with the network team or upstream provider to resolve non-local issues. The essential skill is to interpret ip r and traceroute together to form where the fault lies. Routing and traceroute means use ip r to verify default route and traceroute to pinpoint the hop where traffic stops; combine both to isolate local vs upstream faults.. In practical terms, read the kernel routing table and trace the packet path to find where traffic stops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Route to the root cause
keyIdea.text: Use ip r to verify default route and traceroute to pinpoint the hop where traffic stops; combine both to isolate local vs upstream faults.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Routing and traceroute
Core commands
ip r & traceroute
Read the routing table to confirm default gateways, then use traceroute to observe each hop and locate where the path fails or becomes unexpectedly slow.
$ ip r
default via 192.0.2.1 dev eth0
192.0.2.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link

$ traceroute 8.8.8.8
Supporting points
  • A missing default route prevents access to external networks even when local hosts are reachable.
  • Traceroute shows latency per hop and points to a specific device where packets stop or slow down.
  • Routing problems may require persistent configuration changes via nmcli or network scripts.
Concrete example
If servers can reach local databases but not external APIs, ip r may reveal no default gateway. Adding a gateway or fixing DHCP will restore external access.
Key Takeaway

Routing and traceroute together show whether the failure is local configuration or an upstream network issue requiring coordination.

screens.title: Firewall diagnosis with firewalld
screens.narratorSegment: Firewalls are meant to protect systems but misconfiguration is a frequent cause of blocked services. On Red Hat systems the dynamic manager is firewalld. Start by checking whether firewalld is running with systemctl status firewalld. Next list active zones and their rules with firewall-cmd --get-active-zones and firewall-cmd --list-all --zone=zone_name. If a service is blocked, try adding the service or port temporarily using --add-service or --add-port without --permanent; this lets you test if the firewall is the cause. If the temporary change fixes the issue, then apply the change permanently and reload the service with firewall-cmd --reload. A common mistake is adding a permanent rule and forgetting to reload, or making changes in the wrong zone. Example: if http is blocked, temporarily add http then verify connectivity; once validated add --permanent and reload. Always test firewall changes carefully because incorrect rules can lock you out. If you do lock yourself out, have console or out-of-band access ready before making wide-reaching changes. Firewall diagnosis with firewalld means test with temporary rules first, then apply permanent changes and reload; always verify the correct zone and service before changing rules.. In practical terms, list active zones and rules, test temporary rules, then make permanent changes with reload. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Firewalld workflow
keyIdea.text: Test with temporary rules first, then apply permanent changes and reload; always verify the correct zone and service before changing rules.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Firewall diagnosis
Commands to try
Check firewalld status and zone rules before changing anything. Test temporary rules and only make them permanent after validation.
$ systemctl status firewalld
$ firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
$ firewall-cmd --list-all --zone=public
$ firewall-cmd --add-service=http   # temporary test
$ firewall-cmd --add-service=http --permanent
$ firewall-cmd --reload
Supporting points
  • Temporary rules allow immediate testing without committing changes that could lock you out.
  • Check the correct zone — services may be allowed in a different zone than the interface is bound to.
  • Always reload after applying permanent changes so the runtime and persistent config align.
Common mistake
Forgetting to reload or adding rules to the wrong zone are common errors that leave the service still blocked.
Safety Note

Test changes in a controlled environment and ensure console or out-of-band access before modifying firewall rules on production hosts.

screens.title: Investigating sockets with ss
screens.narratorSegment: Socket inspection reveals whether an application is actually listening on the expected port and shows connection states across TCP and UDP. The ss utility is a modern replacement for netstat and gives detailed output including process IDs and program names when run with -p. A typical command is ss -tunap which lists TCP and UDP sockets, whether they're listening, and which process owns them. This helps answer questions like: is the web server process bound to port 80? Are there many connections stuck in TIME_WAIT? If ss shows no listener on the expected port, the problem is the service configuration or startup, not the network. If the service is listening but connections fail, combine ss with firewall-cmd and ping/traceroute to distinguish local firewall issues from path problems. A common misconception is to assume a listening process implies external accessibility — you must still verify that firewalld allows the port and that routing permits the path. Example: ss -tunap | grep :80 will quickly tell you whether httpd is bound and which PID owns it. What does your socket output tell you about the next diagnostic step?

keyIdea.title: Sockets reveal service state
keyIdea.text: Use ss -tunap to confirm listening sockets, PIDs, and connection states to decide whether a service or network is at fault.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Investigating sockets with ss
Core command
ss -tunap
List TCP and UDP sockets, show listening ports, connection states, and associated processes to determine whether the service is present and healthy.
$ ss -tunap
LISTEN 0      128        0.0.0.0:80      0.0.0.0:*    users:("httpd",pid=1234)
ESTAB  0      0          10.0.0.5:22     10.0.0.2:52344
$ ss -tunap | grep :80
Supporting points
  • If no listener is present, investigate service configuration or startup logs.
  • High counts of TIME_WAIT may indicate many short-lived connections or improper connection reuse.
  • Use the PID in ss output to trace the owning process and check its logs.
Concrete example
ss shows httpd listening on port 80 with PID 1234. If clients cannot connect, check firewalld rules and routing next, since the service is present locally.
Key Takeaway

ss helps you decide whether to fix the application or the network. If a socket is not listening, the network is not the issue.

screens.title: Automating diagnostics with Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible helps you run the same diagnostic checks across a fleet so you can collect consistent evidence quickly. Useful tasks include gathering network facts with the setup module, running dig or nslookup to test name resolution, executing nc to test TCP ports, and listing firewall rules to verify firewalld configuration. Compose these checks into a playbook that registers results and debugs output so you can inspect failures centrally. A common pitfall is assuming playbook tasks run identically across differing host environments; include ignore_errors and changed_when flags where appropriate so the playbook reports status but does not fail early. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Playbook walkthrough
Playbook excerpt
---
- name: Diagnose Database Connectivity from Webserver
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  vars:
    db_host: dbserver1
    db_port: 3306

  tasks:
    - name: Ping database server
      ansible.builtin.ping:
        data: "{{ db_host }}"
      register: ping_result
      ignore_errors: true

    - name: Resolve database server hostname
      command: dig +short {{ db_host }}
      register: dig_result
      changed_when: false
      ignore_errors: true

    - name: Check TCP connectivity to database port
      shell: nc -zvw3 {{ db_host }} {{ db_port }}
      register: nc_result
      changed_when: false
      ignore_errors: true
Supporting explanation
The playbook registers each command result so you can print and analyze them. ignore_errors allows the play to continue gathering data from every host rather than aborting early.
Concrete scenario
Run this playbook from a control host to collect DNS, ping, and TCP connectivity results from webservers. Compare outputs to identify whether failures are local or remote.
Key Takeaway

Use registered outputs to form a remediation plan and avoid making blind changes across production hosts.

Step-by-step checklist
  1. Check interface state and IP with ip a.

Decision grid
Record the first failing layer and act there: interface → DNS → routing → firewall → sockets → application. Fix the lowest failed layer first and re-run the checks.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn a repeatable troubleshooting workflow that helps you find network faults quickly. We'll start with the basics: confirming the interface state and IP addresses, then move through connectivity checks, DNS resolution troubleshooting, routing validation, firewall rule inspection, and socket-level diagnosis. Along the way you will see how to use modern tools like ip, ss, dig, traceroute, firewall-cmd and nmcli, and how to capture and run the same checks across many servers with Ansible. Each tool gives a different clue: interfaces and addresses show what the host knows, ping and traceroute show reachability and path, DNS tools show name resolution behavior, ss reveals what services are listening, and firewall-cmd shows which ports or services are allowed. By combining these clues you can distinguish configuration errors from network outages or service problems. I'll also guide you through a concrete Ansible playbook that automates the checks so you can run diagnostics safely and consistently across your fleet. At the end of the chapter you'll be able to form a hypothesis, test it with commands, and enact safe fixes. What is the first question you will ask when a service becomes unreachable?

By the end of this chapter you will follow a structured troubleshooting flow and use advanced command-line utilities with confidence. You will diagnose network connectivity from the interface up to application sockets, distinguish DNS failures from routing or firewall issues, and verify when a service is actually listening. You will also be able to inspect and adjust firewalld rules safely, and capture the same checks in Ansible playbooks to run them across many servers. These skills reduce the time needed to identify a root cause and help you avoid risky one-off changes. For example, if a web service is unreachable you will know to confirm the interface and IP, test connectivity to the IP, run dig to check name resolution, inspect the routing table for the default gateway, and list firewalld rules to ensure the port is allowed. Finally, you'll be able to automate this sequence so it runs reliably across your fleet. Which diagnostic will you try first when a service fails?

These additional objectives break the chapter into skills you can practice immediately. You will read and manipulate interface state with ip a and ip link set to restore a down interface. You will inspect routing with ip r and use traceroute to discover where packets stop along a path. You will use ss to confirm that services are listening on expected ports and recognize abnormal socket states that indicate overload or stale connections. Finally, you'll author simple Ansible tasks that run dig, check TCP ports, and list firewall rules, giving you repeatable diagnostics across hosts. Practically speaking, this means when a database connection fails you'll try ping to the database IP, run dig against a known DNS server, test TCP connectivity to the port, and confirm local firewall rules. The ability to run those checks from a central control plane reduces manual SSH sessions and improves auditability. Which one of these skills will you practice first?

A basic but crucial diagnostic step is to confirm the local interface state and assigned IP addresses. The command ip a lists each interface, its operational state and configured addresses. Look for the keywords UP or DOWN and for the presence of an expected IPv4 or IPv6 address. If the interface is down you can bring it online with ip link set up. This fixes many simple problems caused by administrative shutdowns, cable issues that have been corrected, or virtual interfaces that were not brought up after a reboot. A common misconception is to assume an interface is up because the service is running; interfaces and services are separate layers. Another frequent oversight is relying on NetworkManager UI without checking the kernel view; ip a shows the kernel's truth. Example: if a web server has no IP address on eth0, adding the address or bringing eth0 up restores reachability and lets you move to the next diagnostic step. After confirming the interface and address, always re-run a connectivity test such as ping to a known good IP. Key takeaway: interface state is the simplest and fastest elimination check before investigating name resolution or routing.

Ping is a basic but powerful tool to check reachability. Use ping to test an IP address first; if that succeeds but pinging a hostname fails, the issue is name resolution. This simple contrast often points directly at DNS. When ping to an IP works, you know the physical path is available and the default gateway and routing likely allow packets out. If ping to an IP fails, investigate the interface, the gateway, and traceroute to find where packets stop. A common misconception is to treat ping failures as proof that the remote host is down; intermediate firewalls or ICMP filtering can block ping while TCP services remain accessible. So, combine ping with a TCP test such as nc -zvw3 host port if ICMP is filtered. Example: you can ping 8.8.8.8 to verify external reachability; if that succeeds but ping example. com fails, use dig against a DNS server to further investigate. Always follow ping with auxiliary checks that test the specific service protocol when ICMP might be blocked. How will you decide whether to test ICMP, DNS, or TCP first in your environment?

DNS issues are a frequent source of application failures because services cannot reach hostnames even when IP connectivity exists. Start by inspecting /etc/resolv. conf to confirm which servers the host will query. If entries are missing or point to unreachable servers, update them or use a specific server for testing. Next, query DNS servers directly with dig or nslookup to verify what the server returns. For example, running dig against a known DNS server isolates whether resolution fails locally or at the server. If dig returns no answer, the DNS server may be misconfigured or unreachable. Local caching can also cause stale answers; use systemd-resolve --flush-caches to clear it when you suspect outdated records. A common misconception is to blame the application when hostnames fail; often the problem is a misconfigured resolver or an unreachable DNS server. Example: if clients cannot resolve api. example. com but resolver shows 127.0.0.53, test dig +short api. example. com @8.8.8.8 to confirm global resolution. Always pair DNS tests with connectivity checks so you know whether DNS or the network path is the root cause.

Routing determines where packets go once they leave your host. Use ip r to inspect the kernel routing table and verify the presence of a default route, typically shown as 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to a gateway. If external hosts are unreachable but local hosts are fine, a missing or incorrect default route is a likely cause. Traceroute helps you locate the hop where packets fail by showing each router along the path and the associated latency. It is particularly valuable for diagnosing problems outside your immediate network, such as an overloaded router or a blocked path. A common misconception is to assume symmetric routing; in reality, routing can differ in return path and an upstream filter may block traffic unevenly. Example: if ip r shows no default gateway, add a temporary route to test connectivity or use NetworkManager tools to persist the change. After identifying the failing hop with traceroute, coordinate with the network team or upstream provider to resolve non-local issues. Firewalls are meant to protect systems but misconfiguration is a frequent cause of blocked services. On Red Hat systems the dynamic manager is firewalld. Remember these practical utilities and behaviors when diagnosing connectivity issues. Use dig or nslookup to test DNS responses and systemd-resolve to flush local caches if entries are stale. For firewall issues on Red Hat, firewalld and firewall-cmd let you inspect zones and test temporary rules; always reload after making permanent changes. Use ss to inspect sockets and identify whether services are listening or whether connection states indicate overload. Finally, automate routine checks with Ansible to collect consistent evidence across hosts. Separating diagnosis from remediation and testing changes temporarily first are small practices that prevent accidental lockouts and make troubleshooting reproducible.
